title: When two sponsors' MAICs disagree: how often, why, and which common target resolves it
question: When two sponsors run MAIC on the same two trials, each weighting its own data to the other trial, how often do their conclusions reverse, how much of that is a real difference in target population rather than sampling error or differing adjustment sets, and which common-target remedy recovers the decision population's effect?
answer: Reversal is mostly a real target difference and it is common: with the modifier's zero-effect point between the two populations, sponsors disagreed in sign in 23% to 56% of analyses at separations up to 1 SD and modification up to 0.4, and moving the point outside the populations cut that by a median 0.31. The two sponsors' estimates are correlated, which a reversal calculation must use. Under linear modification the plain average of the two analyses is as accurate for the midpoint population as transporting both trials there.
findings: Between-minus-outside reversal probability exceeded 0.20 in 11 of 18 common-set configurations (median 0.31); the refuting sentence, that reversals need extreme configurations, fails.
Correlation between the two sponsors' estimates 0.14 to 0.99; a bivariate normal with that correlation predicted the reversal probability within 0.036, and ignoring it erred by up to 0.44.
A sponsor that left the modifier out of its weights was biased by 0.10 to 0.91 against its own target.
Transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses: largest bias 0.024 and 0.027, median RMSE 0.231 and 0.239.
not_answered: Linear modification and a continuous outcome; with nonlinear modification or a non-collapsible scale the average is not the midpoint effect. The arbitrated indirect comparison and measurement differences between trials were not run. Peer review has not been done.
design: Two trials with linear modification of one treatment, analyzed by two sponsors each weighting its own trial to the other's population; 108 scenarios crossing separation, modification strength, the position of the zero-effect point, trial sizes and adjustment sets, plus controls; transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses as remedies.
estimand: B-versus-A mean difference in each sponsor's target population and in a declared decision population
methods_compared: transport of both trials to a declared population
